name: Falam
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Thuan, Khar. 2008. A phonological description of Falam. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. 138 pp. (open PDF with; the Internet Archive copy of the Payap-hosted file)
catalog_locator: Ch. 4 Suprasegmental Phonology, sec. 4.2 Stress, pp. 59-60 (exx. 41-43); restated in ch. 7 Conclusion, sec. 7.1 Summary, p. 94. pp. 59-60 and p. 94 of the copy consulted.
catalog_quote: As defined by Bickford, Falam also has a stress pattern which is hard to distinguish between stress and intonation. Both stress and intonation are meaningful in their context but they are not contrastive. One common stress pattern in Falam is that diphthongs and contrastively long vowels are stressed (ˌ is used for stress marker) as in (41). (41) ˌluaŋ23 ‘to flow’ ˌfiim23 ‘to be wise’ ˌbaaŋ21 ‘to be tired’ ˌnuam21 ‘to be good, to be joyful’ ˌhua⁴⁴ ‘to hate’ ˌjaaŋ⁴⁴ ‘to run’ [p. 59] Stress pattern also occurs when monosyllabic words are attached with nominalizers, /naak⁵²/ and /tuu⁵²/. A nominalized word with two syllables always stresses the second syllable as in (42): (42) /d̪uʔ²¹/ ‘to love’ d̪uʔ²¹ˌnaak⁵² ‘love’ /duʔ²¹/ ‘to love’ duʔ²¹ˌtuu⁵² ‘lover’ /fɛl⁴⁴/ ‘to be honest’ fɛl²¹ˌnaak⁵² ‘honesty’ /lɛj⁴⁴/ ‘to hate’ lɛj⁴⁴ˌtuu⁵² ‘one who buy’ It is proposed that Falam stress pattern always occurs in the last syllable of disyllabic word or trisyllabic word, or even in a final word of connected speech as we will see in the following section. [p. 60] ... [p. 94] There is a relationship between stress and intonation. Stress patterns fall generally upon the second syllable of a compound word consisting of two syllables, and if the word contains more than two syllables, the stress will fall on the last syllable of the word. Being a tonal language, tone is the most fundamental contrastive element in the suprasegmental phonology of Falam.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Falam is a four-tone language (L, H, LH, HL); stress is non-contrastive. In polysyllabic (nominalized or compound) words stress falls on the last syllable: the second syllable of a disyllable, the final syllable of a trisyllable; in connected speech the final word carries the prominence. In monosyllables, long-vowel and diphthong nuclei are heard as stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Author says stress is 'hard to distinguish' from intonation and that neither is contrastive; a separate prominence device is prefixing the vowel /a/ to nouns and adjectives (ex. 43). Monosyllables: only diphthongs and contrastively long vowels are marked stressed (ex. 41).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level for nominalized (-naak, -tuu) and compound di-/trisyllabic words, extended to the final word of connected speech (phrase-level). Auditory analysis by a native-speaker author with recorded 436-item wordlist and texts; tone contours checked in Praat on one speaker. Variety: the Laizo-based Falam common language of Falam Township.
new_statements.identity_note: Thuan 2008 describes 'Falam' = the Laizo-based common language of Falam Township (author is a native speaker; Glottolog fala1243 / ISO cfm covers it directly). King 2010 works with Zahau-dialect consultants; Osburne 1975 and Yip 2004 treat Zahao (Laizo), also under cfm. No separate glottocode needed.

tone_statements.quote: Whereas Hakha Lai and Kuki-Thaadow have only three underlying tones, four tones contrast in Falam. The following examples are from my elicitations (Osburne 1975 reports only three contrasting tones in her study of the Zahao dialect): (23) a. H páa ‘mushroom’ lám ‘road’ b. HL sâa ‘animal’ thlûak ‘brain’ c. LH zu&u ‘bear’ tla&aN ‘mountain’ d. L kèe ‘leg’ sèer ‘lemon’ (p. 197; '&' is the text layer's rendering of the rising-tone diacritic, 'N' of the velar nasal) [p. 192:] As seen, Falam contrasts four tones, while the others contrast only three. They also differ in how stopped tones are realized.
tone_statements.locator: PhonLab Annual Report 8 (2012), p. 192 tables (4)-(5); sec. 3.3 pp. 197-199, exx. (23)-(30)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Four contrastive tones on bimoraic (smooth) syllables: H (paa 'mushroom'), HL (saa 'animal'), LH (zuu 'bear'), L (kee 'leg'); short stopped CVT = L, long stopped CVVT = HL; contours only on bimoraic syllables; LH -> L before H/HL (absorption); LH + L on CV/CVT -> L-H (shift); shortened CV surfaces H (from H, LH) or L (from HL, L) and derived H spreads rightward onto CV/CVC.

sources.note: Secondhand for Falam: four tones H [44], L [21], Rising/Concave [23~323], Falling [52~42] after Thuan 2008; Osburne 1975 posits three underlying tones (L, H, Rising) analysed with [+/-High] per mora; Falam contour restrictions (*LH-H, *HL-L, Hyman 2007), rightward spread onto toneless syllables, H tone marking plural on agreement markers, Stem II verbs restricted to L and HL. General claim: tone is pervasive in SC lexicon and grammar.

sources.note: Places Falam Lai as Type I in a typology of contour-tone distribution: a contour is disallowed before a like tone (*LH-H, LH-L allowed), vs Hakha Lai (before unlike tone) and Thlantlang Lai (before any tone). In Falam only LH tones change: LH -> L before H or HL (tone absorption, tlaang LH + lam H -> tlaang L lam H 'mountain road'); LH + L unchanged if the L is on a smooth syllable, but LH + L on a CV or CVT syllable -> L-H (H shifts right: 'seven mountains', 'mountain pig', 'one mountain'), taken to show that LH requires duration on the FOLLOWING L rime. sources.quote: Primary stems may be L, H, LH or toneless. Underlyingly toneless syllables surface as H after LH, but as L elsewhere. [...] Rising tones are unstable. On short CV syllables, LH becomes H except finally, where the vowel lengthens and the rise survives. (p. 4) | fn. 2: A reviewer points out that his fieldwork has discovered a falling tone in the Zahao spoken in Falam. Many of Osburne's H tones are falls in Falam, which has a four-way L, H, LH, HL distinction. (p. 4)
